Q: What is the difference between transaction isolation levels and optimistic/pessimistic concurrency control? A:

This is one of those topics where the terminology can get really blurry because they both deal with "concurrency," but they operate at different layers. To keep it simple: Isolation Levels are a database-level contract, while Optimistic/Pessimistic Locking are strategies you (the developer) choose to handle specific data integrity scenarios.

1. Isolation Levels (The "Environment" Rules)

Think of Isolation Levels as the "default behavior" of your database. When you set an isolation level (like READ_COMMITTED or REPEATABLE_READ), you are telling the DB engine: "How much do I want to see what others are doing right now?" It’s a global setting for the transaction. The DB uses its internal mechanisms (locks or MVCC) to prevent things like Dirty Reads or Phantom Reads. You don’t usually "code" these; you configure them.

2. Pessimistic vs. Optimistic (The "Strategy" Choice)

These are specific tactics you use for a particular piece of data.

• Pessimistic Locking: You assume the worst. You say, "I’m taking this row, and I don't want anyone else to even touch it until I’m done." It’s like a physical lock on a door. It relies heavily on the DB's internal locking

• Optimistic Locking: You assume everything will be fine. You don't lock the row. Instead, you keep a version number. If someone else updates it while you were working, the DB (or JPA) throws an error when you try to save. This isn't really a DB "lock" in the traditional sense; it's a version check.

Are they independent?

Yes and No. They are complementary.

• You can have a READ_COMMITTED isolation level and still use Optimistic Locking in your Java code to prevent "Lost Updates."

• Actually, in modern web apps, we rarely use the highest isolation level (SERIALIZABLE) because it kills performance. Instead, we use a lower level (like READ_COMMITTED) and handle specific conflicts using Optimistic Locking.

Q: How to unlock my bit locker encrypted drive. A:

Usually if you computer was logged in with microsoft account while encrypting, the key would have got usually got stored on your account.

Link: aka.ms/myrecoverykey or https://account.microsoft.com/devices/recoverykey

After unlocking try to decrypt.

Other way using CMD:

  1. run cmd as administrator.

  2. manage-bde -status use this command to get the status of hardrive.

  3. If the drive is fully encrypted, use manage-bde -off D:. This will start decrypting the drive.

    Usually the process would take time depending on the size of hard drive.
